statuses.meaning: One best answer: the identifier leads to one target in the requested database.
Several genes or targets are equal in all the evidence that decides; all of them are the best answer, in ascending order of gene id and target id.
Genes were reached at the target release, but none of the genes of the best answer has an id in the requested database: the candidates are the genes themselves, never another gene's id.
The identifier is not in the graph: unknown, or of a database the graph does not include.
An Ensembl id or a sequence accession with a version the graph does not hold; the versions that exist are listed (`known_versions`), and no other version's gene is answered.
The identifier is in the graph, but no gene at the target release descends from it (a retired id, for instance); `reasons` says why.
In a batch: the conversion of this identifier raised an error (`error`); the batch went on.

reasons.meaning: The identifier is not an identifier of this graph at any release.
The identifier is an Ensembl id, or a sequence accession, with a version this graph does not hold.
The version written after the accession was not judged: Ensembl's records hold only an edit counter of the records of its database, not a version of the sequence; the accession was read without it.
The identifier is an Ensembl id, not an id of the database named as its source.
The identifier is never active on the assemblies that serve the releases of this graph.
At the release it is read at, the identifier is attached to no gene.
Ensembl's history (and the bridges allowed) leads to no gene at the target release.
The genes reached have no id in the requested database.
The conversion of this identifier raised an error (see `error`).

The graph does not hold the identifier at the release given (`from_release_given`); it was read where the graph holds it (`from_release`), so the targets are what the identifier meant there, which can be another gene than the one it meant at the release given.

step_reasons.meaning: The gene exists at the target release.
The identifier is attached to this gene at the release it is read at.
Ensembl's id history: a new version of the id.
Ensembl's id history: the id was replaced by another.
Ensembl's id history: a split and a merge.
Ensembl re-mapped the gene to itself with a score.
The history reaches no gene at the target release: the walk leaves the gene through an id it carries.
The walk enters another gene that carries the same id.
The gene carries the id in the final database at the target release.
The id is attached at the target release to a transcript or translation the gene had at another release.
Refused: Ensembl's history gives the id of a gene of the mitochondrial genome to a gene of a nuclear sequence, or the reverse; that is no lineage, and the walk does not follow it.

criteria.meaning: The gene is the queried gene id's own version at the target release (an id that exists at the target release is its own answer).

0: the target is attached to the gene at the target release; 1: attached to a transcript or translation that belonged to the gene at another release; `null`: no gene has an id in the requested database and the gene itself is the target.
The bridges through external ids (or shared transcripts) on the path; 0 is Ensembl's history alone.
The releases between leaving a gene and entering the next, summed over the bridges.

The identifier is the display name of an entry gene at the starting release (`gene.display_xref_id`: Ensembl's own name of the gene there, whatever database it came from). Among the genes that carry a name at one release such a gene ranks first, before `entry_support` (`idtrack.engine.ranking`; `decided_by` is `"display_name"` where it decided). It holds for the string as typed: where the string has letters of both cases, only a display name that its database spelt so; a string in one letter case carries no evidence of case and is read without it. Where the history merges several entry genes into `gene`, this and `display_rank` and `entry_support` are the best over all of them, whichever one `entry_gene` names (the path shown starts from one).

The number of databases that attach the identifier to an entry gene at the starting release (1 for an Ensembl id). For an identifier of digits only, databases of other numbers (an NCBI gene id and a Havana number spelt alike) are not counted against each other: their genes tie.
The product of Ensembl's mapping scores along the history of the path (1.0 without a scored event).
The target is the identifier itself (or the gene id it was read as).

`(-external ids, -transcripts, -translations)` of the gene at the target release, where the engine compared it (between successors of one entry gene that are equal in everything else); `null` where it did not.

candidate_fields.meaning: The Ensembl gene (`<id>.<version>`) at the target release through which the target was reached.
The id in the final database, as that database wrote it at the target release (the gene itself for `ensembl_gene`).
Part of the best answer (several candidates are best in a tie).
The gene the identifier was read as at the starting release, from which this gene was reached.

The databases that attach the identifier to the entry gene at the starting release (for an Ensembl id, the Ensembl relation that reads it: `base_ensembl_gene`, ...); a synonym's database by its own name.

A name authority gives the identifier to the entry gene as its symbol at the starting release: HGNC, MGI or VGNC (the symbol databases of the organism) or NCBI's official symbol (`NCBI gene (formerly Entrezgene)`), not as a synonym (such a symbol is read before any synonym of another gene, `idtrack.graph.TheGraph.resolve_name`).

The identifier is the display name of an entry gene at the starting release (`gene.display_xref_id`: Ensembl's own name of the gene there, whatever database it came from). Among the genes that carry a name at one release such a gene ranks first, before `entry_support` (`idtrack.engine.ranking`; `decided_by` is `"display_name"` where it decided). It holds for the string as typed: where the string has letters of both cases, only a display name that its database spelt so; a string in one letter case carries no evidence of case and is read without it. Where the history merges several entry genes into `gene`, this and `display_rank` and `entry_support` are the best over all of them, whichever one `entry_gene` names (the path shown starts from one).

How the identifier is the display name of an entry gene, as the ranking compares it: 0 the display name (for a string in one letter case in an organism whose symbols are written in mixed case, the display name of a name authority, read without letter case); 1 for such a string, the display name of another source; 2 not its display name (`display_name` is `false` only then).

The number of databases that attach the identifier to an entry gene at the starting release (1 for an Ensembl id). For an identifier of digits only, databases of other numbers (an NCBI gene id and a Havana number spelt alike) are not counted against each other: their genes tie.
The gene is the queried gene id's own version at the target release (an id that exists at the target release is its own answer).

0: the target is attached to the gene at the target release; 1: attached to a transcript or translation that belonged to the gene at another release; `null`: no gene has an id in the requested database and the gene itself is the target.
The bridges through external ids (or shared transcripts) on the path; 0 is Ensembl's history alone.
The releases between leaving a gene and entering the next, summed over the bridges.
The product of Ensembl's mapping scores along the history of the path (1.0 without a scored event).

The history steps of the path between two different ids that Ensembl gave no score (it writes 0 where it measured nothing); a path with such a step ranks below every path whose scores are measured, before `score` compares them.
The target is the identifier itself (or the gene id it was read as).
Cross-reference edges on the path.
History edges on the path.

`(-external ids, -transcripts, -translations)` of the gene at the target release, where the engine compared it (between successors of one entry gene that are equal in everything else); `null` where it did not.
With `explain`: the indices of `ExplainedPath.steps` from the identifier to `gene`, in order; empty otherwise.
With `explain`: the indices of the steps from `gene` to `target` (empty when the gene is the target).

match_steps.meaning: The identifier as written (for an external identifier: as a database wrote it at the release read).
The identifier when letter case is ignored.
The identifier when '-', '_' and '.' are taken as one character (and letter case is ignored).
A sequence accession with the version written after it, read where Ensembl's cross references attached that version.
An Ensembl id or a sequence accession with a version newer than every version the graph holds, read as its latest version (an id active, an accession attached, at the graph's last release).
A sequence accession with a version that is not judged: Ensembl's records hold only an edit counter of the records of its database (UniProt's entry version), so the accession is read without it.

match_prefixes.meaning: In a batch: a name made unique by a single-cell tool (another item of the batch with -1, .1 or _1 appended, itself no exact name at the release it is read at alone); the result is that item's.

Unicode was normalised before matching: invisible and control characters (zero-width characters, byte-order marks, bidirectional marks, soft hyphens) removed, compatibility forms (NFKC: full-width letters and digits) and Unicode dashes read as their plain characters.

Stray punctuation was removed before matching: quotes around the identifier, and the punctuation that ends a sentence, a clause or an item of a list at its end (a semicolon, comma, full stop, colon, exclamation or question mark).
GENCODE's form of the Y copy of a pseudoautosomal gene (<id>_PAR_Y) was read as the gene's id; the Y copy is reported apart.
An LRG record's id, answered with the gene the record describes.
A synonym that a database records for the gene, not the name the database gives it.

reading_reasons.meaning: In an organism whose symbols follow a letter-case convention, a string written otherwise that is not exactly a name is read first as a symbol of the organism without letter case, where that names exactly one gene; this reading came after it.

The string ends in a suffix that single-cell tools append to make names unique (-1, .1, _1); reading it, with its separators taken as one or without letter case, as a synonym of another gene than the string before the suffix names is not taken.

The string means this identifier at other releases only (the releases listed), not at the release it was read at: what it meant at another time (a name of one gene then, a synonym of another gene now). Give from_release to read it there.

The string is an identifier followed by a version, and the identifier is, at the release read, also an id of a database that writes its ids without a version (an NCBI gene id spelt like a numeric Havana id of the early releases): where no database has the identifier with that version at that release, the string has two readings, and this is the other one (the identifier as that database's id, without the suffix).
The step that matched reached this identifier as well, at the same release; its candidates are part of the answer, ranked with those of the reading taken by the same evidence of lineage.

place_relations.meaning: On one assembly the two genes overlap (one sequence region, one strand), or a place carried onto the other's assembly by Ensembl's mapping of the two assemblies overlaps it.

On one assembly the two genes do not overlap: another sequence region, another strand, or apart; or a place carried onto the other's assembly by Ensembl's mapping of the two assemblies shares no base with it; or a copy's reference region (Ensembl's assembly exception) shares no base with the other gene; or, on two assemblies that no published mapping joins, they lie on chromosomes of different names (the mitochondrial genome against a chromosome among them), which no assembly change turns one into the other.
The two genes never lie on one assembly at the same time, and nothing tells them apart (a sequence of one name, or a scaffold): their places cannot be compared.

A gene lies outside the reference sequence (a patch, a haplotype, an alternative locus, an LRG record), and nothing places it apart from the other gene (it lies inside its assembly exception's reference region, or it is an LRG record, which has none): its place is not compared base by base with the reference sequence.
The graph holds no place for one of the two genes.

bridge_rules.meaning: Taken: the two genes overlap on one assembly, or Ensembl's mapping of their two assemblies carries one onto the other.
Taken: the places of the two genes cannot be compared (two assemblies, a sequence of one name or a scaffold), and no release gives the id to both: the id left one gene for the other.

Taken: a gene lies outside the reference sequence (a copy on a patch, a haplotype, an alternative locus, an LRG record), where places are not compared, both genes carried the id at one release, and at every such release the genes that carried it are one gene: the copy and the gene it stands for.
Refused: a synonym is no bridge (it names other genes too often to stand for one).

Refused: on one assembly the two genes do not overlap, or Ensembl's mapping of their two assemblies carries one elsewhere, or a copy's reference region does not hold the other gene, or on two assemblies that no published mapping joins they lie on chromosomes of different names.
Refused: the graph holds no place of a gene (a graph made in memory) and both genes carry the id at one release, so it names two living genes, not one gene that became the other.

Refused: a gene lies outside the reference sequence, where places are not compared, and at a release at which both genes carried the id it named several genes (a family label, a shared alias): it does not say which gene the copy stands for.

Refused: the two genes share a stable id that Ensembl gave first to a gene of the mitochondrial genome and then to a gene of a nuclear sequence (or the reverse); they are two genes, and no id makes one the other (the history step between them is refused alike).

Refused: a gene lies outside the reference sequence, and no release gave the id to both genes: a copy stands for the gene that carries its names while it exists, not for a gene the id reached at another time.

errors.title: The request is not in the form the endpoint takes.
errors.meaning: The request does not have the shape the endpoint takes: a missing or malformed parameter, a body that is not UTF-8 JSON of the documented shape (`details` lists each problem, `argument` names the parameter when one is at fault).

errors.title: The request names a parameter the endpoint does not take, or names one twice.
errors.meaning: A query parameter the endpoint does not take, or one given more than once.

errors.title: An identifier is too long, or holds characters an identifier cannot hold.
errors.meaning: An identifier or name is longer than this server accepts, or holds control, surrogate, private-use or unassigned characters (in a batch: the whole batch is refused, and `details` gives every such item's index).

errors.title: A release this graph does not cover.
errors.meaning: A release the graph does not cover (`allowed` lists the graph's releases).

errors.title: A database this graph does not hold at that release.
errors.meaning: A database the graph does not hold at that release (`allowed` lists those it holds).

errors.title: An identifier this graph does not hold.
errors.meaning: An identifier the call needs to exist in the graph does not (the gene of names-of).

errors.title: An identifier is empty, or stands for a missing value.
errors.meaning: An identifier is empty or a spelling of a missing value (idtrack's refusal), or a name to look up is empty.

errors.title: A value this endpoint does not accept.
errors.meaning: An argument whose value is not accepted (an empty or over-long database name).

errors.title: An input idtrack does not accept.
errors.meaning: Another input idtrack refuses (idtrack's message says which).

errors.title: An organism this server does not hold.
errors.meaning: An organism this server does not hold (`allowed` lists those it holds).

errors.title: Nothing is at this address.
errors.meaning: No such endpoint or file.

errors.title: This address does not take this kind of request.
errors.meaning: The endpoint does not take this method (the `Allow` header and `allowed` list the methods it takes).

errors.title: The request did not arrive in time.
errors.meaning: The request's head or body did not arrive within the time the server waits for it, or its client closed the connection before its search (which is then not run); send it again.

errors.title: The request is larger than the server accepts.
errors.meaning: The request body is larger than the server accepts.

errors.title: More identifiers than one batch may hold.
errors.meaning: A batch with more identifiers than the server accepts (`batch_max` of /limits).

errors.title: The address is longer than the server accepts.
errors.meaning: The request's path and query are longer than the server accepts.

errors.title: The request's body is not JSON.
errors.meaning: A request body that is not `application/json` in UTF-8, or that is sent compressed (`Content-Encoding`).

errors.title: One identifier's search needed more than its budget.
errors.meaning: One identifier's search needed more than its budget (states or seconds); the same request fails again.

errors.title: The answer is larger than the server sends.
errors.meaning: The answer is larger than the server sends (`response_max_bytes` of /limits); it is refused, never cut.

errors.title: Too many requests from this address for now.
errors.meaning: This client sent more requests, or used more search time, than its allowance; wait the `Retry-After` header's seconds.

errors.title: A fault of the server.
errors.meaning: A fault of the server; quote the request id when reporting it.

errors.title: The server is busy.
errors.meaning: The server has more waiting work than it accepts: its queue of searches is full, the search would wait (or waited) longer for a worker than `queue_seconds` of /limits, or the server is stopping; the request was not searched. Retry after the `Retry-After` header's seconds, unchanged.

errors.title: The search needed more time than one request may take.
errors.meaning: The request's search needed more time than its budget (`request_seconds` of /limits, counted from when its search began); send fewer identifiers per request (a batch's message says how many it converted).

database_kinds.meaning: One of idtrack's two Ensembl gene namespaces: `ensembl_gene`, the gene id with its version, and `base_ensembl_gene`, without (`versioned` says which).
An external database whose ids are accessions (NCBI's gene numbers in `EntrezGene`, RefSeq's and UniProt's accessions); where the graph holds its labels apart, `labels` names their database.

An external database whose ids are labels (display names, symbols) rather than accessions (the graph's `label_databases`): a name authority's symbols, NCBI's official symbols, UniProt's gene names; `labels_of` names the accession databases whose labels it holds.

allowances.meaning: Searching requests (`rate_per_minute` per minute, `rate_burst` at once).
Every other request of the api (`read_share` times the searches' allowance).
Seconds of search (`rate_search_seconds` per minute, a balance of `rate_search_burst_seconds`).
Searching requests in progress at once (`rate_concurrent_searches`).

source_modes.meaning: An origin is a release (counted only on the assembly that serves it).
An origin is a genome assembly (its number in idtrack's organism table).
An origin is `[assembly, release]`: the release and the genome assembly it was read on.

cautions.meaning: The best answer is reached through a bridge: where Ensembl's history gives a gene no successor, the walk left it through an id it carries and entered another gene that carries the same id. That is idtrack's inference; no record of Ensembl states it.

A bridge on the best answer's path joins two genes that lived at the same releases: the gene it enters did not take the place of the gene it leaves in Ensembl's records, so their shared ids are no sign of succession.
The bridge taken enters the gene nearest in releases, while another gene, reached by a bridge from the same gene through ids the bridge taken does not pass, ranks below by the bridge's gap alone.
A step of Ensembl's history on the best answer's path joins two genes that do not lie at one place: the walk follows Ensembl's record, which moved the gene.
Steps of the best answer's path join genes that never lie on one assembly at the same time: where Ensembl publishes no mapping of the two assemblies, their places cannot be compared.
Every gene of the best answer lies outside the reference sequence at the target release (on a haplotype, a patch or an alternative locus): the answer holds no gene of the reference sequence.

The identifier is a bare number, read in every database whose ids are numbers, and the graph holds it only at an earlier release than the target: it was read as an id of a database of that time, which may not be the one meant. Name the database as `from_database` to read it in one database only.
The best answer's path holds history steps between two different stable ids to which Ensembl gave no score.
The id in the database asked is attached, at the target release, to a transcript or translation the gene had at another release, not to the gene itself.
The graph does not hold the identifier at the release given; it was read at another release, where the graph holds it: the answer is what the identifier meant there.
The identifier was read as a synonym, not as the name or id itself.
The item was read as the copy of another item of the batch (a name with `-1`, `.1` or `_1` appended).
The identifier matched only without letter case.
The identifier matched only with its separators taken as one.
The identifier's version is newer than any version the graph holds: it was read as the latest version held.
At other releases the same string names another gene (or reads as another id): a list made at that time means that gene. Read it at such a release (`from_release`) to have what it meant then.
The same string is also read as another id, with another answer.
The best answer is also listed among the copies the result sets apart (`alternative_locus_genes`): the answer is the gene, and code that drops the genes of that list would drop it.
The identifier is a bare number, read in every database whose ids are numbers; name the database as `from_database` to read it in one database only.
The targets are every id the best gene carries in the database asked: idtrack converts at the level of the gene, not the counterpart of the identifier alone.

The best answer descends through a split of Ensembl's history, and other successors were reached: idtrack ranks the successors of a split by Ensembl's scores and the candidates' evidence, not by which of them lies where the old gene lay.
The same string is also read as another id at the same step.
The identifier's version was not judged (`version_not_judged`).
The identifier was read after a Unicode normalisation.
The identifier was read with punctuation removed.
A gene's copy on the Y chromosome's pseudoautosomal region was read as its gene.
An LRG record was read as its gene.
The lowest of Ensembl's mapping scores on the best answer's path, stated exactly (the candidate's score is the product of the scores along its path).
